info.name: Open Life Quoting API (AU)
info.description:
A vendor-neutral contract for pricing Australian life risk cover.

Set `baseUrl` and `accessToken` in the collection variables before sending. The default `baseUrl` points at this contract's local mock — `npm run mock` serves it on port 4010. Request bodies, where an operation takes one, are the contract's own worked examples: validated against the schema and posted at a live mock in CI, so they are known to be accepted.

variable.description: An implementation's base URL. Defaults to this contract's local mock (`npm run mock`, port 4010) so the collection is usable before you have an insurer endpoint.
OAuth2 client-credentials access token. The mock accepts any non-empty value.

header.description: A consumer-generated UUID identifying this logical request. Replaying the same key with an identical body MUST return the stored response rather than re-pricing; replaying it with a different body MUST fail with 409 `idempotency-conflict`. Servers SHOULD retain keys for at least 24 hours.
Consumer-supplied correlation identifier. Echoed on the response; the server generates one if absent.

request.description:
Price the requested covers for one insured and return every line the insurer can offer, plus the lines it had to decline.
### What a response means
One request yields MANY lines. An insurer with two brands and a campaign on one of them may answer a single life-cover request with three lines. Consumers must treat the response as a set of comparable offers, never as "the price".
### Three things a consumer must not do
- **Do not derive a frequency.** `annual / 12` is not the monthly premium, because sub-annual
  premiums carry a frequency loading. Every line carries `monthly` and `annual`; the other four
  appear only where the insurer quotes them, and the ones it does not are named in
  `premiums.not_quoted`. An absent frequency cannot be bought at any price, so a derived figure
  is both wrong and unpurchasable.
- **Do not price a failed line.** A line with `all_needs_met: false` carries no `premiums` and
  is not an offer. It exists so the adviser can see that this insurer was asked and could not
  write the combination.
- **Do not assume an option was applied.** Check `resolved_options`. An option the product
  cannot honour appears there as `unsupported_ignored`, and the premium does not include it.

### Caching
Quote responses carry personal information about the insured and MUST NOT be cached by intermediaries. Servers MUST send `Cache-Control: no-store`.

header.description: Consumer-supplied correlation identifier. Echoed on the response; the server generates one if absent.

request.description:
Describe the covers, option values, brands, campaigns and optional features this implementation offers.
A consumer calls this once and caches it. It drives which controls an adviser is offered, so an unsupported combination can be prevented rather than rejected after the fact.
This is the mechanism that makes a partial implementation conformant: an insurer that writes four covers and three waiting periods declares exactly that, and the conformance suite tests it against what it declared rather than against the whole standard.
Consumers MUST NOT treat this document as authoritative. Hand-maintained capability documents drift from the pricing engine, so the runtime paths — 422 `unsupported-value` and `resolved_options` — stay mandatory regardless of what is declared here.

item.name: Search this insurer's own occupation list

header.description: Consumer-supplied correlation identifier. Echoed on the response; the server generates one if absent.

query.description: Free-text search over the insurer's own occupation descriptions. Matching is implementation-defined; servers SHOULD match on substrings of any word rather than a prefix of the whole string, since advisers search on the distinguishing word ("painter") rather than the leading one.
The insured's gross annual income, so the insurer can return the occupation row that actually applies to them.
Continuation token from the previous page's `page.next_cursor`.
Maximum items per page. A server MAY return fewer for its own reasons, so completion is signalled only by the absence of `page.next_cursor`.

request.description:
Return the occupations this insurer rates, in its own wording, each with its rating matrix.
This exists so an adviser can correct one insurer's occupation by hand. The usual flow resolves an occupation once via `POST /occupations:match`, but where the match is imperfect — or where the adviser knows this insurer's product better — they need to search the insurer's own list and choose. That choice is then sent as `occupation.insurer_occupation_id` on the next quote, and the insurer rates on it without re-matching.
Returning the rating matrix inline is deliberate: it lets a consumer show the consequence of a change before spending a pricing call on it.
An empty `q` returns the whole list, paged, so a consumer can pre-load it.

item.name: Resolve a baseline occupation to this insurer's own

header.description: Consumer-supplied correlation identifier. Echoed on the response; the server generates one if absent.

request.description:
Given an ABS OSCA code and the qualifiers that sit beneath it, return the insurer's own occupations that correspond, most confident first.
### Why this endpoint exists
An adviser picks an occupation once, from one picker, and expects to compare every insurer on the panel. Each insurer rates its own list, so something has to bridge the two. Putting the bridge here — inside the insurer, which is the only party that knows its own manual — avoids making anyone else the custodian of a mapping they cannot maintain.
### An empty result is a real answer
`candidates: []` means this insurer has no occupation corresponding to the reference. The consumer MUST show the insurer as unquotable for this client and MUST NOT substitute a nearby occupation of its own choosing. A silently wrong occupation produces a wrong premium that looks entirely normal, and an adviser has no way to detect it.
### Confidence
Where the insurer maintains a one-to-one correspondence to the baseline it returns `exact`. A match derived from qualifiers alone will usually be `moderate` or below, and a consumer SHOULD ask the adviser to confirm anything below `exact` rather than pricing straight through.
Results depend only on the occupation reference, never on the insured, so they are safely cacheable by the consumer per insurer.
